Well-differentiated small hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is generally considered to be an early-stage cancer. This means that it has a good prognosis, and the disease is likely to respond well to treatment.

In clinical practice, the absence of significant differences in disease-free survival rates between patients with well-differentiated HCC and those with less differentiated HCC (low-grade or intermediate-grade) suggests that well-differentiated HCC can be considered clinically early cancer. This is because even though there may not be a significant difference in outcomes, the cancer still has a high likelihood of being curable.

Well-differentiated small hepatocellular carcinoma typically represents an early-stage tumor with a low risk of spread and aggressive behavior. It is often diagnosed at an early stage when the cancer is still localized to one lobe of the liver, making it easier to treat.

The fact that an increase in circumference measurements identified the most potential lymphedema cases compared to other studies suggests that early detection of changes in lymphatic function can help identify individuals with a higher risk of developing lymphedema. However, further investigation is needed to determine whether this approach should be adopted as a routine diagnostic tool.

Overall, well-differentiated small hepatocellular carcinoma has an excellent prognosis when diagnosed at an early stage and treated appropriately.
